documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
**DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN**

- Work Part A first. You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example,

Doe, Jamie

A1 – 1/3

- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. It may not be used in graphing mode. Calculators may not be shared. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas. You may use a ruler or straight edge.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Good luck!

problems.statement: An empty 4.2-g balloon is filled with air to a pressure of 2.0 atm at the ambient temperature of $20.0^\circ$ C. When filled it is spherical with a radius of 15.0 cm. The mean molecular mass of air is 28.8 g/mole and the atmospheric pressure is $1.01\times10^5$ Pa.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: The filled balloon is weighed by placing it on a scale. What is the scale reading?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: The filled balloon is now gently heated until its radius increases by 10%. What is the scale reading now?

solution.statement:
Let $R=0.15\text{ m}=$ the radius of the balloon

$p=2\times1.01\times10^5\text{ Pa}=$ The pressure inside the balloon

$m_b=0.0042\text{ kg}=$ The mass of the empty balloon

$T=(20+273)\text{ K}=$ The temperature of the air

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
The volume of the balloon is $V=\frac43\pi R^3=\frac43\pi(0.15\text{ m})^3=0.0141\text{ m}^3$.

Using the ideal gas law

$$n=\frac{pV}{RT}=\frac{(2.02\times10^5\text{ Pa})(0.0141\text{ m}^3)}{(8.31\text{ J/mole}\cdot\text{K})(293\text{ K})}=1.17\text{ moles}.$$

Therefore the mass of the air inside the balloon is

$$m=nM=(1.17\text{ moles})(28.8\text{ g/mole})=33.7\text{ g}=0.0337\text{ kg}.$$

The scale reading will be equal to the force of gravitational attraction $(m+m_b)g$ on the balloon and the enclosed air minus the buoyant force $B=m_{dis}g=\rho gV$ acting on the balloon, where $m_{dis}$ is the mass of the air displaced by the balloon.

$$F_s=(m+m_b)g-m_{dis}g=(m+m_b-m_{dis})g.$$

The temperature and volume of the air displaced is the same as that of the air within the balloon but the pressure is only half as much.

$$m_{dis}=n_{dis}M=\tfrac12nM=\tfrac12m=0.0168\text{ kg}.$$

$$F_s=(0.0337\text{ kg}+0.0042\text{ kg}-0.0168\text{ kg})(9.8\text{ m/s}^2)=0.21\text{ N}.$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
The amount of air inside the balloon and its mass do not change. The volume of air displaced and its mass both change by the amount

$$m'_{dis}=\rho V'=\rho\tfrac43\pi(R')^3=\rho\tfrac43\pi(1.1R)^3=(1.1)^3\rho\tfrac43\pi R^3=(1.1)^3m_{dis}=(1.1)^3(0.0168\text{ kg})=0.0224\text{ kg}.$$

$$F_s=(m+m_b-m'_{dis})g=(0.0337\text{ kg}+0.0042\text{ kg}-0.0224\text{ kg})(9.8\text{ m/s}^2)=0.15\text{ N}.$$

problems.statement:
The circuit diagrammed at the right consists of a 6.0-V power supply and eight 12.0-$\Omega$ resistors, labeled 1–8.

[[figure:p2-fig1]]

figures.alt: 6.0-V supply and eight resistors labelled 1 through 8.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the equivalent resistance of the circuit?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the current in each resistor? Please use $I_j$ to denote the current in resistor $j$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Resistors 1, 5, and 7 are replaced with 4.0-$\mu$F capacitors. What is the charge on each capacitor after the circuit has been connected for a very long time? Please use $Q_j$ to denote the charge on the capacitor in location $j$.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: The capacitor in location 5 is replaced with a second 6.0-V power supply (positive end closest to resistor 3 and negative end closest to resistor 6). What is the current through each resistor after the circuit has been connected for a very long time? Please use $I_j$ to denote the current in resistor $j$. In this part 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8 denote 12.0-$\Omega$ resistors, 1 and 7 denote 4.0-$\mu$F capacitors, and 5 denotes a 6.0-V power supply.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Because of symmetry, $I_1=I_2$ and $I_4=I_5$ and $I_7=I_8$.

No current flows through 3 or 6. $I_3=0$ and $I_6=0$.

1, 4, and 7 are effectively in series with an equivalent resistance of $R_s=R+R+R=3R$.

Similarly for the right branch containing 2, 5, and 8.

The left and right branches are in parallel so, the equivalent resistance is given by

$$\frac1{R_{eq}}=\frac1{3R}+\frac1{3R}=\frac2{3R}$$

or

$$R_{eq}=\frac{3R}{2}=\frac{3(12\,\Omega)}2=18\,\Omega.$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
As stated in the argument in Part a. $I_3=0$ and $I_6=0$. All the other currents are equal $I_1=I_2=I_4=I_5=I_7=I_8=I$.

Applying Kirchhoff’s loop rule to the left loop

$$0=6.0\text{ V}-I(3R),\qquad I=\frac{6.0\text{ V}}{3R}=\frac{6.0\text{ V}}{36\,\Omega}=\frac16\text{ A}.$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
When the circuit has been connected for a very long time, the capacitors are fully charged. No current flows through 1, 5, and 7. There is only one path for the current, through 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8. These five resistors are effectively in series with

$$V_R=(1/5)\,6.0\text{ V}=1.2\text{ V}$$

across each. Applying Kirchoff’s loop rule to the upper loop $0=V_R+V_R-V_{C1}$

$$Q_1=CV_{C1}=C\,2V_R=(4.0\,\mu\text{F})(2.4\text{ V})=9.6\,\mu\text{C}$$

Similarly for $Q_7=9.6\,\mu\text{C}$.

For the middle loop we have $0=V_R+V_R+V_R-V_{C5}$

Which yields $Q_5=CV_{C5}=C\,3V_R=(4.0\,\mu\text{F})(3.6\text{ V})=14.4\,\mu\text{C}$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
When the circuit has been connected for a very long time, no current flows through 1 or 7. The same current flows through 3, 4 and 6.

$$0=6.0\text{ V}-3RI,\qquad I_3=I_4=I_6=\frac{6.0\text{ V}}{36\,\Omega}=\frac16\text{ A}.$$

There is 2.0 V across each of the resistors 3, 4, and 6 and capacitors 1 and 7. Hence the voltage across 2 and 8 is zero and $I_2=I_8=0$.

problems.statement:
A relativistic particle decays into two photons. One of the photons is traveling to the right along the x-axis with frequency $
u_1$. The second photon is traveling to the left with frequency $
u_2$, where $
u_1>
u_2$. Express your answers to the following in terms of given quantities and known constants.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the velocity $V$ of the original particle.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the rest mass of the original particle.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: What are the frequencies of the photons in the rest frame of the original particle? What are their directions of travel in this rest frame?

parts.label: d.
parts.statement:
You are given the following formula:

$$p'_x=F_1p_x+F_2\frac{E_\gamma}{c}$$

where $p'_x$ is the observed x-component of the momentum of either photon, whereas $E_\gamma$ and $p_x$ are the energy and x-component of the momentum of the photon in the rest frame of the particle. Using your results determine the functions $F_1$ and $F_2$ in terms of $V/c$, where $V$ is the speed of the original particle.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
The relativistic energy and momentum of a particle are given by

$$E=\frac{mc^2}{\sqrt{1-(V/c)^2}},\qquad p=\frac{mV}{\sqrt{1-(V/c)^2}}$$

where $m$ is the particle mass and $V$ is the particle speed. The energy and momentum of a photon of frequency $\nu$ are given by

$$E_\gamma=h\nu,\qquad p_\gamma=\frac{h\nu}{c}.$$

Applying energy conservation, we have

$$\frac{mc^2}{\sqrt{1-(V/c)^2}}=h\nu_1+h\nu_2\tag{A3.1}$$

while momentum conservation gives

$$\frac{mV}{\sqrt{1-(V/c)^2}}=\frac{h\nu_1}{c}-\frac{h\nu_2}{c}.\tag{A3.2}$$

Dividing (A3.2) by (A3.1), we have

$$\frac{mV}{mc^2}=\frac{h(\nu_1-\nu_2)}{ch(\nu_1+\nu_2)}.$$

Canceling common factors and solving for $V$

$$V=c\frac{\nu_1-\nu_2}{\nu_1+\nu_2}\quad\text{to the right}.\tag{A3.3}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Writing the given equation for photon 1

$$\frac{h\nu_1}{c}=F_1\frac{h\nu}{c}+F_2\frac{h\nu}{c}=(F_1+F_2)\frac{h\nu}{c}$$

Or

$$(F_1+F_2)=\frac{2h\nu_1}{mc^2}.\tag{A3.5}$$

While for photon 2

$$-\frac{h\nu_2}{c}=-F_1\frac{h\sqrt{\nu_1\nu_2}}{c}+F_2\frac{h\sqrt{\nu_1\nu_2}}{c}$$

or

$$(F_1-F_2)=\frac{2h\nu_2}{mc^2}\tag{A3.6}$$

Adding (A3.5) and (A3.6)

$$2F_1=\frac{2h}{mc^2}(\nu_1+\nu_2)$$

$$F_1=\frac1{\sqrt{1-(V/c)^2}}.$$

Subtracting (A3.6) from (A3.5) we have

$$2F_2=\frac{2h}{mc^2}(\nu_1-\nu_2)$$

and comparing to (A3.2)

$$F_2=\frac{(V/c)}{\sqrt{1-(V/c)^2}}$$

problems.statement:
Two movable wedges of mass $M$ meet the horizontal plane smoothly. They are free to slide without friction on the plane. See accompanying diagram. A coin of mass $m$ is released from rest at the height $h$ and slides down the left hand wedge. Assume that the coin always slides without friction. Express your answers to the following in terms of given quantities and known constants.

[[figure:p4-fig1]]

figures.alt: Coin m at height h on two movable frictionless wedges of mass M.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the maximum height the coin will rise on the right-hand wedge?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: For what minimum mass $M$ will the coin again contact the left-hand wedge?

solution.statement:
Since friction is assumed non-existent, all collisions are elastic. Both momentum and mechanical energy are conserved.

Let $v=$ speed of coin after it has left the left-hand wedge

$V_L=$ speed of left-hand wedge after coin has left

$H=$ maximum height the coin reaches on the right-hand wedge

$V=$ speed of right-hand wedge and coin when coin is at its highest point on the right-hand wedge and at rest with respect to it

In all of the following, velocities to the right will be positive and velocities to the left will be negative. Equating the energy and momentum of the initial condition (coin at height h) and final condition (coin has completely left left-hand wedge).

Momentum conservation

$$0=-MV_L+mv$$

Solving for $V_L$

$$V_L=\frac mM v\tag{A4.1}$$

Energy conservation

$$mgh=\tfrac12MV_L^2+\tfrac12mv^2$$

Substituting (A4.1)

$$2mgh=M\left(\frac mMv\right)^2+mv^2=m\left(\frac mM+1\right)v^2$$

Solving for $v^2$

$$v^2=\frac{2Mgh}{m-M}\tag{A4.2}$$

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Equating the energy and momentum of the initial condition (coin with velocity v, right-hand wedge at rest) and final condition (coin at rest with respect to right-hand wedge).

Momentum conservation

$$mv=(m+M)V\tag{A4.3}$$

Energy conservation

$$\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12(m+M)V^2+mgH\tag{A4.4}$$

Combining (a4.3) and (A4.4)

$$mv^2=(m+M)\left(\frac m{m+M}v\right)^2+2mgH=\frac{m^2}{m+M}v^2+2mgH$$

Solving for $H$

$$H=\frac1{2g}\left(1-\frac m{m+M}\right)v^2=\frac1{2g}\left(\frac M{m+M}\right)v^2$$

Substituting (A4.2) into this

$$H=\frac1{2g}\left(\frac M{m+M}\right)\left(\frac{2Mgh}{m+M}\right)=\left(\frac M{m+M}\right)^2h.$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Let $v_F=$ The speed of the coin after it has left the right-hand wedge

$V_R=$ The speed of the right hand wedge after the coin has slid off it

For the coin to again contact the left-hand wedge $v_F>V_L$. Equating the momentum and energy before and after the coin’s collision with the right-hand wedge

Momentum conservation

$$mv=MV_R-mv_F$$

$$V_R=\frac mM(v+v_F)$$

Energy conservation

$$\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12MV_R^2+\tfrac12mv_F^2$$

Combining the last two equations and dividing by $m$ and multiplying by 2.

$$v^2=\left(\frac mM\right)(v+v_F)^2+v_F^2$$

$$Mv^2=m(v^2+2vv_F+v_F^2)+Mv_F^2$$

Or regrouping terms

$$0=(M+m)v_F^2+(2mv)v_F-(M-m)v^2$$

Solving this quadratic equation for $v_F$

$$v_F=\frac{-2mv\pm\sqrt{(2mv)^2+4(M+m)(M-m)v^2}}{2(M+m)}=\frac{-2mv\pm\sqrt{4M^2v^2}}{2(M+m)}=\frac{-mv\pm Mv}{(M+m)}$$

Only the plus sign gives a positive speed and a velocity in the correct direction.

$$v_F=\left(\frac{M-m}{M+m}\right)v$$

For the coin to again contact the left-hand wedge $v_F>V_L$, or

$$\left(\frac{M-m}{M+m}\right)v>\frac mMv$$

Dividing by $v$ and cross multiplying, the condition becomes

$$(M-m)M>(M+m)m$$

Or

$$M^2-2Mm-m^2>0$$

Using the quadratic formula this becomes

$$M>\tfrac12\left(2m\pm\sqrt{4m^2+4m^2}\right)$$

Since M must be positive this becomes $M>m(1+\sqrt2)$

problems.statement: A hollow spherical shell of radius $b$ and negligible thickness is constructed out of insulating material with total charge $-Q$. A second similar shell has radius $c$ where $c>2b$ and total charge $+Q$. Each shell has its charge distributed uniformly over its surface. Assume the electrostatic potential is zero at infinity. As shown at the right, the symbols I, II, and III may be used to denote the regions inside the smaller shell, between the shells, and outside the larger shell, respectively. Express your answers to the following in terms of given quantities and known constants. You may use either spherical or Cartesian coordinates.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Because the charge distribution is uniform, there is spherical symmetry and we can use Gauss’s Law to calculate the electrostatic field. This yields

$$\vec E=k\frac{q_{enc}}{R^2}\vec e_R$$

where $R=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$, $q_{enc}$ is the charge enclosed by a Gaussian surface of radius R, and $\vec e_R$ is a unit vector in the $\boldsymbol{R}$ direction.

Region I: A Gaussian surface of radius $R<b$ encloses no charge, so $E_I=0$

Region II: A Gaussian surface of radius $c>R>b$ encloses $q_{enc}=-Q$

Thus

$$\vec E_{II}=-k\frac{Q}{R^2}\vec e_R\qquad\text{or}\qquad E_{II}=k\frac{Q}{R^2}\ \text{ radially inward.}\tag{B1.1}$$

Region III: A Gaussian surface of radius $R>c$ encloses $q_{enc}=-Q+Q=0$

Therefore $E_{III}=0$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Region III: Since the field is zero, the potential is a constant throughout the region. Its value at any point in III is the same as its value at infinity $V_{III}=0$

Region II:

$$V_{II}(R)-V_{II}(c)=-\int_c^R\vec E\cdot d\vec l$$

Using (B1.1), $d\vec l=(-\vec e_R)(-dR)=\vec e_RdR$, and noting $V_{II}(c)=V_{III}(c)=0$

$$V_{II}(R)=\int_c^Rk\frac{Q}{r^2}\,dr=\left.-k\frac{Q}{r}\right|_{r=c}^{R}=k\frac{Q}{c}-k\frac{Q}{R}=kQ\left(\frac1c-\frac1R\right)$$

Region I: Since the field is zero, the potential is constant and is everywhere equal to its value on the boundary $V_I=V_{II}$ at $R=b$. Thus $V_I=kQ\left(\frac1c-\frac1b\right)$.

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
In each region the total field can be obtained by superposition, adding vectorially the fields due to the individual spheres. $\vec E=\vec E_{+Q}+\vec E_{-Q}$.

Inside each uniformly charged sphere the field due to that sphere is zero.

Region I: This region is inside both spheres so both contributions are zero and $E_I=0$.

Region II: The field due to the $+Q$ sphere is zero in this region. The field due to the $-Q$ is equivalent to that due to a $-Q$ point charge at $x=0$, $y=0$, $z=b$. Letting $\vec R=x\hat i+y\hat j+(z-b)\hat k$ represent the vector from this point charge to the arbitrary field point, we have

$$\vec E_{II}=-\frac{kQ\vec R}{R^3}=\frac{kQ(x\hat i+y\hat j+(z-b)\hat k)}{[x^2+y^2+(z-b)^2]^{3/2}}.$$

Region III: In this region both spheres contribute to the field. Adding to the previous result the contribution equivalent to a $+Q$ point charge at the origin, yields

$$\vec E_{III}=-\frac{kQ(x\hat i+y\hat j+(z-b)\hat k)}{[x^2+y^2+(z-b)^2]^{3/2}}+\frac{kQ(x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k)}{[x^2+y^2+z^2]^{3/2}}.$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Region III: Since the field here is the equivalent to that due to two point charges, so is the potential.

$$V_{III}=kQ\left(\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}-\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-b)^2}}\right).$$

Region II: In this region, the contribution due to the inner sphere is equivalent to that due to a point charge. The contribution due to the outer sphere is constant. To find this value, equate across the boundary with Region III.

$$V_{II}=kQ\left(\frac1c-\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-b)^2}}\right).$$

Region I: Since the field is zero, the potential is constant. To find this value, equate across the boundary with Region II.

$$V_I=kQ\left(\frac1c-\frac1b\right).$$

sections.title: a–b
sections.statement:
The spherical shells are concentric as shown in Figure a. at the right.

[[figure:p5-fig1]]

figures.alt: Figure a. Concentric spherical shells, radii b and c, charges -Q and +Q, regions I, II, III and axes.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the electrostatic field in regions I, II, and III as a function of position.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the electrostatic potential in regions I, II, and III as a function of position.

sections.title: c–d
sections.statement:
The spherical shells are not concentric as shown in Figure b at the right. The inner shell is shifted in the positive $z$ direction a distance $b$ equal to its radius.

[[figure:p5-fig2]]

figures.alt: Figure b. Inner charged spherical shell displaced a distance b in the positive z direction.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Find the electrostatic field in regions I, II, and III as a function of position.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Find the electrostatic potential in regions I, II, and III as a function of position.

problems.statement:
We shall model a car as a uniform rectangular block of length $L$ and height $h$ with mass $M$ that has struts of length $R$ that rest on the frictionless axles of two wheels of radius $R$, one front wheel and one rear wheel. Each wheel has a mass $m$ and a uniform mass density. The driver can exert a friction force at the top of the front wheel to slow down the car. See the diagram below.

[[figure:p6-fig1]]

Assume that the two identical wheels have a coefficient of static friction $\mu$ with the ground. The driver applies a braking force that causes the vehicle to decelerate with a deceleration of magnitude $a$.

figures.alt: Car block M of length L and height h, wheels m and radius R, velocity and front-wheel friction brake.
Rear-wheel rotation with angular velocity, angular deceleration and ground friction.
Rear-wheel translation with axle force, friction and acceleration.
Front-wheel rotation showing brake and ground friction.
Front-wheel translation showing brake, ground friction, axle force and acceleration.
Carriage free-body diagram with length, heights, weight, normal and horizontal forces.
Front-wheel vertical forces nF, NF and mg.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
For the wheel $I=\tfrac12mR^2$ and $a=\alpha R$ since it is rolling without slipping. The wheel is turning clockwise. It’s decelerating so the force producing the torque must be towards the front of the car. For the rotational motion of the rear wheel about its axis

[[figure:p6-fig2]]

$$I\alpha=f_RR$$

$$\tfrac12mR^2\frac aR=f_RR$$

Therefore

$$f_R=\tfrac12ma\qquad\text{toward the front.}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Now consider the translational deceleration of the rear wheel

[[figure:p6-fig3]]

$$ma=F_{CR}-f_R$$

where we have chosen the acceleration direction to be positive. Therefore

$$F_{CR}=ma+f_R=ma+\tfrac12ma=\tfrac32ma\qquad\text{towards the rear.}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
Consider the total external force acting on the car-wheel combination which has total mass $M+2m$

$$f_F-f_R=(M+2m)a$$

$$f_F=f_R+(M+2m)a=\tfrac12ma+(M+2m)a=\left(M+\tfrac52m\right)a\qquad\text{towards rear.}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Considering the rotational motion of the front wheel about its axis

[[figure:p6-fig4]]

$$I\alpha=(f_B-f_F)R$$

$$\tfrac12mR^2\frac aR=(f_B-f_F)R$$

Solving for $f_B$

$$f_B=\tfrac12ma+f_F=\tfrac12ma+\left(M+\tfrac52m\right)a=(M+3m)a$$

towards the rear.

sections.title: e.
sections.statement:
Consider the total external force acting on the front wheel

[[figure:p6-fig5]]

$$f_F+f_B-F_{CF}=ma$$

$$F_{CF}=f_F+f_B-ma=\left(M+\tfrac52m\right)a+(M+3m)a-ma=\left(2M+\tfrac92m\right)a$$

towards the front.

sections.title: f.
sections.statement:
We will first calculate the normal forces exerted by the axles on the carriage part of the car. Call these normal forces $N_R$ and $N_F$. Using Newton’s third law to find the horizontal forces exerted on the carriage by the axles and the brake, we have the force diagram at the right.

[[figure:p6-fig6]]

Consider the vertical forces acting on the block part of the car. There is no acceleration in the vertical direction, so these must sum to zero. Or

$$N_F+N_R=Mg.\tag{B2.1}$$

Consider the torques acting on the block part of the car. It is not rotating, so the total torque about the center of mass must equal zero.

$$F_{CR}\left(\frac h2+R\right)+f_B\frac h2+N_F\frac L2-F_{CF}\left(\frac h2+R\right)-N_R\frac L2=0$$

Rearranging terms

$$N_F-N_R=\frac2L\left[(F_{CF}-F_{CR})\left(\frac h2+R\right)-f_B\frac h2\right]$$

Substituting the known $F_{CF}$, $F_{CR}$, and $f_B$

$$N_F-N_R=\frac2L\left[\left(2M+\frac92m-\frac32m\right)a\left(\frac h2+R\right)-(M+3m)a\frac h2\right]$$

$$N_F-N_R=\frac aL[(2M+3m)(h+2R)-(M+3m)h]=\frac aL[hM+2R(2M+3m)]\tag{B2.2}$$

Adding (B2.1) and (B2.2)

$$2N_F=\frac aL[hM+2R(2M+3m)]+Mg$$

$$N_F=\frac12Mg+\frac{ah}{2L}M+\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)$$

And for the rear axle

$$N_R=Mg-N_F=\frac12Mg-\frac{ah}{2L}M-\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)$$

These are the upward forces exerted by the axles on the carriage. Consider now the vertical forces acting on the wheel, shown in the diagram at the right. Since there is no vertical acceleration these must sum to zero.

[[figure:p6-fig7]]

$$n_F-N_F-mg=0$$

Finally

$$n_F=N_F+mg=\frac12(M+2m)g+\frac{ah}{2L}M+\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)\tag{B2.3}$$

Similarly for the rear wheel

$$n_R=\frac12(M+2m)g-\frac{ah}{2L}M-\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)\tag{B2.4}$$

sections.title: g.
sections.statement:
For each wheel the maximum frictional force corresponding to the maximum deceleration is $\mu n$. For the rear wheel $f_R=\mu n_R$.

Using the results of Part a and Part f.

$$\frac12ma=\mu\left[\frac12(M+2m)g-\frac{ah}{2L}M-\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)\right]$$

Solving for a

$$a_{R\max}=\frac{\mu(M+2m)gL}{mL+\mu[Mh+(2M+3m)2R]}\tag{B2.5}$$

For the front wheel $f_F=\mu n_F$

$$\left(M+\frac52m\right)a=\mu\left[\frac12(M+2m)g+\frac{ah}{2L}M+\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)\right]$$

$$a_{F\max}=\frac{\mu(M+2m)gL}{(2M+5m)L-\mu[Mh+(2M+3m)2R]}\tag{B2.6}$$

sections.title: h.
sections.statement:
Putting the given values into (B2.5) and (B2.6), we have

$$a_{R\max}=\frac{0.6(6000\text{ kg}+2(200\text{ kg}))g(2.5\text{ m})}{(200\text{ kg})(2.5\text{ m})+0.6[(6000\text{ kg})(1.5\text{ m})+(2(6000\text{ kg})+3(200\text{ kg}))2(0.3\text{ m})]}$$

$$a_{R\max}=0.920g$$

$$a_{F\max}=\frac{0.6(6000\text{ kg}+2(200\text{ kg}))g(2.5\text{ m})}{(2(6000\text{ kg})+5(200\text{ kg}))(2.5\text{ m})-0.6[(6000\text{ kg})(1.5\text{ m})+(2(6000\text{ kg})+3(200\text{ kg}))2(0.3\text{ m})]}$$

$$a_{F\max}=0.425g$$

therefore the maximum deceleration the car can have is $a_{\text{car}\max}=0.425g$

sections.title: i.
sections.statement:
Forming the ratio and substituting in the given values

$$\frac{n_F}{n_R}=\frac{\frac12(M+2m)g+\frac{ah}{2L}M+\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)}{\frac12(M+2m)g-\frac{ah}{2L}M-\frac{aR}{L}(2M+3m)}=\frac{(M+2m)gL+ahM+2aR(2M+3m)}{(M+2m)gL-ahM-2aR(2M+3m)}$$

$$\frac{n_F}{n_R}=\frac{(6000\text{ kg}+2(200\text{ kg}))g(2.5\text{ m})+(0.425g)(1.5\text{ m})(6000\text{ kg})+2(0.425g)(0.3\text{ m})(2(6000\text{ kg})+3(200\text{ kg}))}{(6000\text{ kg}+2(200\text{ kg}))g(2.5\text{ m})-(0.425g)(1.5\text{ m})(6000\text{ kg})-2(0.425g)(0.3\text{ m})(2(6000\text{ kg})+3(200\text{ kg}))}$$

$$\frac{n_F}{n_R}=\frac{(6400\text{ kg})(2.5\text{ m})+(0.425)(1.5\text{ m})(6000\text{ kg})+2(0.425)(0.3\text{ m})(12600\text{ kg})}{(6400\text{ kg})(2.5\text{ m})-(0.425)(1.5\text{ m})(6000\text{ kg})-2(0.425)(0.3\text{ m})(12600\text{ kg})}$$

$$\frac{n_F}{n_R}=2.57$$

sections.title: a–g
sections.statement: Express your answers to the following in terms of given quantities and known constants.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find $f_R$ the frictional force of the ground on the rear wheel.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find $F_{CR}$ the horizontal component of the force exerted by the car on the axle of the rear wheel.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Find $f_F$ the frictional force of the ground on the front wheel.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Find $f_B$ the force of the brake that is applied to the front wheel.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Find $F_{CF}$ the horizontal component of the force exerted by the car on the axle of the front wheel.

parts.label: f.
parts.statement: Find $n_F$ and $n_R$ the normal forces exerted by the ground on the front and rear wheels.

parts.label: g.
parts.statement: For each wheel, find the maximum possible deceleration of the car before that wheel starts to slip.

parts.label: h.
parts.statement: Numerically evaluate the magnitude of the maximum possible deceleration of the car in terms of the acceleration of gravity, $g$.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Numerically evaluate the ratio of the normal force of the ground on the front wheel to that on the rear wheel at this maximum deceleration.
